issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Anh's Vigil

Anh Pham was thirty-eight when a man with a knife took his wallet outside the hospital where he worked. It happened on a Tuesday evening in March, in the employee parking lot behind the medical center, as Anh was walking to his car after a twelve-hour shift in the cardiac ward. The attacker came from behind the concrete pillar between rows four and five-a place Anh had passed a thousand times without thinking. The knife appeared first, a silver flash that caught the overhead light. The man's face was obscured, but his voice was clear: Give me your wallet. Anh's hands shook as he complied. The man took it and ran. No one was hurt. The police found nothing. Within days, the incident report was filed and the hospital's risk management team sent an email about increased security measures. Life continued.

But Anh's life did not.

In the weeks that followed, sleep became impossible. He would lie beside his wife Maria for hours, his mind replaying the moment the knife appeared-not as a sequence of events, but as a series of photographs, each one crystalline and unbearable. The image of the silver blade. The attacker's hand. His own reflection in the car window. These images did not fade; they remained as vivid as if he were looking at actual photographs. When he finally did sleep, he would wake gasping, feeling a sharp pain in his ribs and across his shoulders, the exact places where his muscles had tensed during those seconds of terror. Maria would reach for him in the dark, but he could not explain that his body was reliving something his mind could not escape.

Returning to work became an exercise in hypervigilance. In the hospital corridors, Anh found himself constantly scanning the faces of visitors and staff, assessing each person for threat. In the break room, he could not sit with his back to the door; he would arrive early to claim the chair that faced the entrance, the one where he could see anyone approaching. His colleagues noticed that he seemed distracted, always looking over his shoulder, always tense. One of the senior nurses asked if he was all right. He said yes. He was not all right.

The parking lot became impossible. For two months, Anh took the bus to work, a forty-minute commute that stretched his already exhausted schedule. But the bus itself triggered the same scanning behavior-he sat near the driver, watching the street, watching the other passengers, his jaw clenched the entire ride. When the hospital finally installed additional lighting in the parking lot, Maria urged him to drive again. He tried once. He made it as far as row three before the panic seized him, and he turned around and went home. He called in sick. He began calling in sick more often.

At home, Anh had come to check mirrors compulsively-the rearview mirror when he was driving, the hallway mirror when he came inside, the bathroom mirror before bed. He was not sure what he was looking for. His own face, perhaps, or evidence of someone behind him. He kept his mind occupied constantly: podcasts during breakfast, audiobooks while showering, television or music playing at all times. Silence was unbearable because silence meant the images would return. Maria noticed he was always doing something, always in motion, always distracted. She asked him to be present, to sit with her without the noise. He could not. The moment the background sound stopped, the photograph of the knife blade appeared in his mind, and with it came the phantom pain across his ribs.

Six months into this, Anh had come to believe that something intrinsic to him had invited this violence-that there was something in the way he walked, the way he held himself, some invisible mark that had made him a target. He had convinced himself that nothing good could happen anymore, that the world had revealed itself as fundamentally dangerous and that he was fundamentally vulnerable. His future, which had once included promotions and travel with Maria, now seemed to contain only more vigilance, more fear, more nights without sleep. He had not been back to the parking lot in four months. His supervisor had begun documenting his absences.

It was Maria who finally made the appointment. She told Anh that she could not watch him disappear anymore, that whatever had happened in that parking lot was still happening, and that he needed help to stop it. At forty-four, sitting in the therapist's office, Anh described the photographs in his mind and the pain in his body and the certainty that he had somehow deserved this, that nothing good awaited him. He did not know if he could return to the parking lot, to his car, to the life he had before. He only knew that he could not continue living like this-trapped between the image of a knife and the conviction that he was marked for harm.
